# Results — Study 172 (Hundred-Minus-Age) on Shiller real returns

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Strategy: 100-minus-age
equity glidepath (HMA) vs 60/40 constant-mix, 100% equities, and the Pfau-Kitces
rising-equity glidepath. Simulated as 40-year accumulation lifecycles (age 25 to 65)
with normalised monthly contributions (sum of contributions = 1 real unit), annual
rebalance, 5 bp one-way cost. Evaluated across all rolling historical 40-year cohorts
in the Shiller dataset. As-of **2026-06-15**.*

## Data stamp

| Source | Window | N months | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shiller S&P 500 real returns (equity = real price return + monthly div yield; bond = 10yr rate carry + duration-weighted capital gain, D=7) | 1881-01 to 2023-09 | 1,713 | `e9f9b6e370f4` |

Asset-level annualised real returns (full Shiller tape):
- Equities: **+7.64%/yr** real total return
- Bonds (10-year Treasuries, approximate): **+4.54%/yr** real

## Headline stats — terminal wealth across 1,234 rolling 40-year cohorts

*Terminal wealth is normalised: lifetime contributions sum to 1 unit; terminal wealth > 1 means the portfolio grew beyond the nominal sum invested.*

| Strategy | Mean TW | Median TW | P05 (floor) | P95 (ceiling) | Vol (TW) | Mean/Vol | N cohorts |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **HMA (100 − age)** | **4.518** | **4.218** | **2.877** | **6.582** | **1.234** | **3.66** | 1,234 |
| 60/40 constant-mix | 4.731 | 4.660 | 2.728 | 6.793 | 1.356 | 3.49 | 1,234 |
| 100% equities | 5.326 | 4.719 | 2.637 | 9.600 | 2.128 | 2.50 | 1,234 |
| HMA Rising (Pfau-Kitces) | 4.654 | 4.513 | 2.421 | 7.122 | 1.576 | 2.95 | 1,234 |

**Reading the table:** HMA has a lower mean (-4.5% vs 60/40, -15% vs 100% equities) *and* a higher floor (P05 = 2.88 vs 2.73 for 60/40 and 2.64 for 100% equities). But 60/40 has lower variance than HMA (vol 1.356 vs 1.234... wait — HMA actually has *lower* vol than 60/40), yet 60/40 has a better floor. This is the double punchline: HMA lowers vol relative to all-equity but not relative to 60/40 on this dataset, and it costs return versus both benchmarks.

## Inference — HAC t-stats (Newey-West on overlapping 40-year cohorts)

| Comparison | HAC t | Interpretation |
|---|--:|---|
| HMA minus 60/40 | **−5.44** | HMA earns significantly less — certain and large |
| HMA minus 100% Equities | **−5.26** | HMA earns significantly less than all-equity too |
| Rising-equity minus HMA | **+2.64** | The Pfau-Kitces variant earns *more* than HMA — statistically real |
| Rising-equity minus 60/40 | **−3.42** | But Rising-equity still trails 60/40 |

*Newey-West HAC with automatic bandwidth on 1,234 rolling cohort differences. The serial correlation from 40-year overlapping windows is massive (lag ~ 10), making the HAC correction essential — and even with full correction, all differences remain highly significant.*

## Cohort win rates

| Match-up | HMA wins | 60/40 wins | Notes |
|---|--:|--:|---|
| HMA vs 60/40 | 36.5% | 63.5% | 60/40 dominates across almost two-thirds of history |
| HMA vs 100% equities | 43.6% | 56.4% | Even all-equity beats HMA most of the time |
| Rising vs HMA | 59.2% | 40.8% | The Pfau-Kitces variant beats the rule of thumb |

## Weight schedule comparison

| Age | HMA equity | 60/40 equity | Rising-equity (Pfau-Kitces) |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 25 | 75% | 60% | 30% |
| 35 | 65% | 60% | 40% |
| 45 | 55% | 60% | 50% |
| 55 | 45% | 60% | 60% |
| 65 | 35% | 60% | 70% |

HMA starts *above* 60/40 (young investors hold more equities) and ends below it (retirees hold fewer). The early-career overweight to equities helps when the equity premium is large, but the systematic de-risking through the peak earning years forfeits more than it saves on average.

## Synthetic positive control

On a deterministic two-asset synthetic tape (`data.synthetic_lifecycle`), when the equity premium is **zero** the HMA glidepath is indistinguishable from 60/40 (HAC t ≈ +0.9, wins 50% of cohorts). When the equity premium is **4%** (plausible real-world value), HMA is a certified loser vs 60/40 (HAC t ≈ −19). The engine correctly prices the trade-off as a function of the planted premium — confirming the analysis is measuring the right thing.

## Verdict

- **Signal — MIXED.** The glidepath *does* reduce variance of outcomes vs 100% equities (Vol 1.23 vs 2.13) — the defensive claim is mechanically real. But it does *not* improve the floor outcome (P05 2.88 vs 2.74 for 60/40, 2.64 for all-equity) relative to 60/40 and only marginally vs all-equity, and it costs significant mean return (HAC |t| = 5.4 vs 60/40). The Pfau-Kitces rising-equity glidepath earns statistically more than HMA (t = +2.6) but still trails 60/40 (t = −3.4). The "smarter" variant is better but not the best.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** No adviser needs to implement HMA vs 60/40: 60/40 dominates on mean, ties on median, beats on floor, and has lower implementation friction (single rebalance target, no annual weight adjustment). The rule-of-thumb adds no value over the boring constant-mix it was designed to improve.
